title: Thomson's Plum-Pudding Model and its Failure
topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: The model Rutherford disproved. Knowing exactly what Thomson's atom predicted — and which prediction failed — shows why the α-scattering result was so decisive.

J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 from cathode-ray studies: cathode rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields, so they are negatively charged particles, and their charge-to-mass ratio e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ is the same for every cathode material — electrons are universal constituents of all atoms. Since atoms are neutral, positive charge had to exist somewhere.
• The atom is a sphere of positive charge with radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m — the size of the whole atom.
• Electrons are embedded in it like plums in a pudding (or seeds in a watermelon), arranged to minimise their mutual repulsion.
• Total positive charge = total negative charge → the atom is neutral.
• Mass is spread uniformly through the sphere; electrons are held by electrostatic forces and can oscillate about their positions — which is how Thomson tried to explain light emission.

• Prediction: positive charge is diffuse, so an α-particle (mass 4 u, charge +2e) passing through should experience many small, cumulative deflections — large-angle scattering should be vanishingly rare.
• Observation: ≈1 in 8000 α-particles is deflected by more than 90°, and some bounce straight back.

• Conclusion: the model is untenable — the positive charge must be concentrated in a tiny, massive nucleus. Rutherford said it was 'as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you'.
• It was the first model built on measured particles (e/m, charge of the electron from Millikan's oil-drop experiment, 1909).
• It correctly demanded neutrality and electron arrangement, and it could explain single small-angle scattering.
• Its failure set the two requirements every later model must meet: explain atomic stability and discrete line spectra.

Dalton (indivisible atom) → Thomson (electrons in diffuse positive sphere) → Rutherford (nuclear atom) → Bohr (quantised orbits) → quantum-mechanical model (orbitals). Each model keeps the successes of the previous one and repairs one specific failure.
confusion: ❌ Thomson discovered the proton along with the electron. ✅ Only the electron (1897); the proton was identified by Rutherford in 1919.
❌ The plum-pudding model explained the line spectrum of hydrogen. ✅ It could not; oscillating electrons would give a continuous spectrum.
❌ Thomson's model placed the nucleus at the centre. ✅ It had no nucleus at all — positive charge was spread over the whole atom.

universalFacts: Thomson's e/m value is identical for every cathode material — the evidence that electrons are universal building blocks.
Rutherford's '15-inch shell' remark refers to the improbability of back-scattering in a diffuse-charge atom.
The oil-drop experiment (Millikan, 1909) fixed the electron's charge, completing Thomson's picture.
examples: **Problem:** Why could small-angle scattering be explained by Thomson's model? **Solution:** a uniform positive charge density gives each passing α-particle a small, smoothly varying electrostatic impulse; summed over ≈1000 atoms the net deflection stays small — consistent with most α-particles passing nearly straight through.

summary: Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 — cathode rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields, so they are negatively charged particles, and their e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ is the same for every cathode material, so they are universal constituents. Since the atom is neutral, positive charge had to exist, and in 1904 Thomson proposed the plum-pudding (watermelon) model: a sphere of positive charge of radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m, the size of the whole atom, with electrons embedded like plums in a pudding, mass spread uniformly and electrons oscillating about their positions to emit light. Its prediction failed decisively. Diffuse positive charge should produce only many small cumulative deflections, yet ≈1 in 8000 α-particles was deflected by more than 90° and some rebounded, which Rutherford likened to firing a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and having it return. The positive charge had to be concentrated in a tiny massive nucleus.
importantConcepts: Background: cathode rays (Thomson, 1897) are negative particles with a gas-independent e/m, so electrons are universal
The 1904 plum-pudding model: sphere of diffuse positive charge of radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m with electrons embedded in it
Mass spread uniformly through the sphere; electrons held electrostatically and oscillating to emit light
Prediction: only small, cumulative deflections, so large-angle scattering should be vanishingly rare
Observation: ≈1 in 8000 α-particles beyond 90° and some back-scattered — the model is untenable
importantStatements: Thomson's model was the first built on measured particles, using the e/m ratio and Millikan's charge of the electron (1909).
The model had no nucleus at all: the positive charge was spread over the entire atomic volume.
It could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen, since oscillating electrons would radiate a continuous spectrum.
Small-angle scattering was consistent with the model, since a uniform charge density gives small smooth impulses.
The chain runs Dalton → Thomson → Rutherford → Bohr → quantum-mechanical model, each repairing one specific failure.

keyPoints: Frame the model as the hypothesis under test in the α-scattering experiment.
Diffuse charge cannot produce back-scattering; a concentrated nucleus can.
The '15-inch shell at tissue paper' remark captures the improbability of 180° scattering.
Every later model had to satisfy two requirements: explain stability and explain discrete line spectra.
specialNotes: Do not confuse the plum-pudding model with Dalton's indivisible atom, which had no substructure at all.
Thomson discovered the electron only; the proton was identified by Rutherford in 1919.
Oscillating electrons in the model were Thomson's attempt to explain light emission, and they predict a continuous spectrum.
